meta.ogDescription: Franklin never said it. Wikiquote flags it as misattributed; the earliest trace is a 1951 column, itself wrongly crediting Tytler.

answer.label: Not Benjamin Franklin — a 20th-century misattribution
answer.sourceLine: This line appears in the “Misattributed” section of Wikiquote’s Benjamin Franklin page, which states there is “no evidence that Franklin ever actually said or wrote this.” It is a modern paraphrase of an idea whose earliest documented appearance is a 1951 newspaper column — and that older version was itself wrongly credited to Alexander Fraser Tytler ↗, in whose works it has never been found.

source.heading: A quote with no author — and no source before 1951

docMeta.dd: “This Is the Hard Core of Freedom,” The Daily Oklahoman, 9 Dec 1951

source.excerpt: When the people find that they can vote themselves money, that will herald the end of the republic.
trail: Wikiquote files this exact line under Misattributed on its Benjamin Franklin page ↗, noting “no evidence that Franklin ever actually said or wrote this.”

The closest older version was credited to Alexander Fraser Tytler in Elmer T. Peterson’s column “This Is the Hard Core of Freedom” in The Daily Oklahoman (9 Dec 1951) — the earliest documented occurrence ↗.
Wikiquote records that the passage “has not been found in Tytler’s works,” so even the Tytler credit is unsupported; the underlying idea echoes Polybius’s Histories ↗.
source.excerptNote: No such sentence appears in Franklin’s letters, essays, almanacs, or recorded speeches. The related, differently-worded passage that circulated first read: “A democracy…can only exist until the majority discovers it can vote itself largess out of the public treasury” — credited in 1951 to Tytler, not Franklin.
source.rightsNote: The exact wording is an anonymous modern paraphrase with no identified author or first-publication source before the mid-20th century, so no copyright or public-domain status can be responsibly asserted. It is not a genuine Franklin text.

author.name: Benjamin Franklin
author.heading: About Benjamin Franklin
author.bio: Benjamin Franklin was a printer, scientist, diplomat, and signer of the Declaration of Independence and the U.S. Constitution — and, as author of Poor Richard’s Almanack, one of America’s most quotable figures. That fame makes him a magnet for invented “Founder” quotations. This warning about voting oneself money is one of them: it matches neither his documented views nor any text in his voluminous published papers, and did not surface until more than 160 years after his death.

misattribution.heading: A fake Franklin quote with a tangled family tree
misattribution.intro: This is a classic “Founder’s-quote” fabrication: a punchy political warning pinned onto Benjamin Franklin to borrow his authority. The wording has no source in anything Franklin wrote, and the idea itself has been passed around under at least three different famous names.

items.why: Wikiquote lists “When the people find that they can vote themselves money, that will herald the end of the republic” in its Misattributed section ↗, stating there is “no evidence that Franklin ever actually said or wrote this.”

items.scope: The older ‘largess from the public treasury’ version
items.why: The related passage was credited to Tytler in a 1951 newspaper column, but Wikiquote notes the quotation “has not been found in Tytler’s works ↗.”

Wikiquote observes the line is “remarkably similar” to a quote “often attributed, without proper sourcing, to Alexis de Tocqueville and Alexander Fraser Tytler” — none of the three attributions is documented in the named author’s writings.

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest documented appearance of this idea is Elmer T. Peterson’s 1951 column in The Daily Oklahoman — over a century and a half after Franklin’s death — per Wikiquote ↗.

context.heading: Why this quote sticks to Franklin
lead: The sentiment — that democracies self-destruct once voters learn to reward themselves from the treasury — is an old one, with echoes as far back as the Greek historian Polybius. But the crisp, modern English sentence circulated today has no author earlier than the 1950s.

Attaching it to Benjamin Franklin gives a contemporary political argument the weight of a Founding Father. That is exactly the pattern behind most fake “Franklin,” “Jefferson,” and “Tytler” quotations: the words are real enough as an argument, but the attribution is decorative, not documentary.
context.pull: No author before 1951 — and even then, credited to the wrong man.
